standard.goal: Developers read a UX document when they design the product, build it and judge a change to it. From it they build a product that gives its users what they come for, by the path the document shows.

template.skeleton:
# <Product name> UX

## OKRs

- O1: <What a user gets from the product, in one short sentence with the user as its subject>
  - KR1.1: <A result that shows O1 is closer, and which direction is better>
  - KR1.2: <Another such result>

Key results have no target values. When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure (Goodhart's law). Use the key results to judge how close the objective is.

## Scenarios

<Each participant and its kind: a person, an AI or a script>

### O1: <A short name for how the user reaches O1>

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  <Who does what, in order, from the first request to reaching O1>
```

parts.what: The OKRs section: the objectives, each with its key results, and the fixed paragraph on target values.
parts.why: Developers, deciding what to build next, see which one objective a piece of work serves.

parts.what: O1, O2, ...: one short sentence of what a user gets from the product, with the user as its subject.
parts.why: Developers, asked who the product is for, answer with the user and what they get, and judge each piece of work by it.

parts.what: KR1.1, KR1.2, ... under each objective: a result that shows the objective closer, and which direction is better.
parts.why: Developers, after a change, see whether users came closer to the objective.

parts.what: The Scenarios section: the participants, then one scenario for each objective.
parts.why: Developers, building toward any objective, find how users reach it.

parts.what: The paragraph at the start of Scenarios: each participant and whether it is a person, an AI or a script.
parts.why: Developers, building a step, see whether it waits for a person or runs on its own.

parts.what: A section headed with an objective's ID, holding a sequence diagram of the main path from the user's first request to reaching it.
parts.why: Developers, building toward that objective, see who does what, in order.

checklist.what: When the developer decides what to build next, can they tell from the OKRs which one objective the work serves?
checks: Does each objective say something no other objective says?
Does every objective have its key results under it?
checklist.why: Developers weigh each piece of work by the objective it serves. Where each objective says something of its own and has its key results, a piece of work serves one, and developers see how it is measured.

examples.fails: O1: A worker books a room quickly. O2: A worker finds a free room easily. (A faster search serves both, so no one can tell which it moves.)
examples.passes: O1: An office worker books a room that fits their meeting, without asking anyone. O2: A facilities manager sees which rooms go unused.

checklist.what: When a colleague asks "Who uses this product, and for what?", can the developer answer from the objectives?
checks: Is the objective's subject a user?
Does it say what that user gets, not what the product does?
checklist.why: Everything developers design and build serves these objectives. If each objective says in one short sentence what a user gets, with that user as its subject, developers know who the product is for and when it has done its job. An objective written as a product feature, or as the way the product gives it, can be met while the user is no better off.

examples.fails: O1: The app shows each room's free times and takes bookings.
examples.passes: O1: An office worker books a room that fits their meeting, without asking anyone.

grounds: ISO 9241-11:2018, 3.1.1: usability is the "extent to which a system, product or service can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use".
Christensen, Hall, Dillon and Duncan, "Know Your Customers' 'Jobs to Be Done'", Harvard Business Review, 2016: a job is the progress a person is trying to make, not a feature of the product.

checklist.what: When a colleague asks "Did this change make things better for users?", can the developer answer by the key results?
checks: Does each key result count a signal that the user is closer to the objective?
Does it say which direction is better?
Does it carry no target value?
checklist.why: Developers improve the product by moving its key results. If all of them getting better means users are closer to the objective, that work helps users. A key result chosen because it is easy to count, such as tasks done or items produced, can improve while users get nothing more. A key result given a target value, rather than the direction that is better, is worked toward the number instead of toward users.

examples.fails: KR1.1: Bookings made per week; more is better. (More bookings can mean more double bookings and rebookings.)
examples.passes: KR1.1: The share of meetings held in the room booked for them, without a double booking or a room change; higher is better. KR1.2: The time from opening the app to a confirmed booking; shorter is better.

grounds: Rodden, Hutchinson and Fu, "Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications", CHI 2010: each metric is derived from a goal through a signal of success toward it (Goals-Signals-Metrics).
Strathern, "Improving ratings: audit in the British University system", European Review, 1997, stating Goodhart's law: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure."

What Matters (whatmatters.com), "What is an OKR? OKR Meaning, Definition & Examples": "Most of all, they are measurable and verifiable. You either meet a Key Result’s requirements or you don’t — there is no gray area, no room for doubt."

checklist.what: When the developer builds toward any objective, do they find the scenario of how users reach it?
checks: Does every objective have a scenario headed with its ID?
checklist.why: Developers build each objective by its scenario. An objective with no scenario is built by guesswork or not at all.

examples.fails: Two objectives and one scenario, so how a facilities manager sees unused rooms is shown nowhere.
examples.passes: A scenario headed O1 and one headed O2.

checklist.what: When the developer builds a step of a scenario, can they tell from the participants whether it waits for a person or runs on its own?
checks: Is each participant named with its kind: a person, an AI or a script?
Do the diagrams use only these names?
checklist.why: A step that waits for a person is built with a way to ask them, and one that runs on its own is built to run unattended. Where every participant's kind is named, developers build each step the right way.

examples.fails: Participants: the worker and RoomBook, so whether the rooms that fit are chosen by a person, an AI or a script is said nowhere.
examples.passes: Participants: the worker, a person; RoomBook, a script.

checklist.what: When a colleague asks "Who does what, from the user's first request until this objective is reached?", can the developer answer from the objective's scenario?
checks: Does the scenario start at the user's first request?
Does it end where the user has what the objective says?
Does it show each step between, with who takes it?
checklist.why: Developers build what the scenarios show. Where a scenario runs from the user's first request to reaching the objective, every step is built on purpose. A step the scenario skips is built by guesswork or not at all.

examples.fails: A scenario that starts when the app receives a booking, skipping how the worker finds a room that fits.
examples.passes: The worker enters the time and the number of attendees, RoomBook shows the rooms that fit, the worker books one and sees it in their calendar, and finds the room free at meeting time.

grounds: Cockburn, Writing Effective Use Cases, 2000: the main success scenario runs from the trigger to the goal delivered, and a use case names its actors first.

checklist.what: When the developer changes how the product is built, can they leave this document as it is?
checks: Does the document say only what users do, see and receive?
Does it name no component, store or call inside the product?
checklist.why: How the product is built belongs in the architecture document. If this document describes only what users do, see and receive, developers can choose the best design and still deliver the UX. Internal design written here is decided twice, drifts from the architecture document, and crowds out the user experience.

examples.fails: A scenario in which the app queries the database for free slots and caches the result.
examples.passes: The same scenario: the worker asks for rooms at a given time and sees which are free. How the app finds them is left to the architecture document.

grounds: ISO 9241-210:2019: user requirements are specified from the context of use before design solutions are produced.
